contractor-agreement-clauses.x: [vCISO / Advisory Firm] Template Notice

This template is provided for example purposes only and does not constitute or represent a complete agreement or supplement legal advice. It is recommended that an organization's independent legal counsel review this agreement before adopting the language or entering into any agreements utilizing the language.
AMENDMENT TO AGREEMENT

This Amendment (the “Amendment”) is entered into as of [Effective Date] by and between [Company Name], a [State/Country] [Corporation/LLC/Entity Type] with its principal place of business at [Company Address] (“Company”), and [Contracting Firm Name], a [State/Country] [Corporation/LLC/Entity Type] with its principal place of business at [Contracting Firm Address] (“Contractor”).
WHEREAS, Company and Contractor entered into an agreement dated [Original Agreement Date] (the “Agreement”); and
WHEREAS, the parties desire to amend the Agreement to include additional obligations related to information security and personnel security.
NOW, THEREFORE, in consideration of the mutual covenants and agreements contained herein, the parties agree as follows:
1. Information Security Responsibilities

Contractor shall be responsible for implementing and maintaining appropriate administrative, technical, and physical safeguards to protect the security, confidentiality, and integrity of Company’s information, systems, and data, including but not limited to:
1.1 Workstation and Endpoint Security Management
Contractor shall ensure that all endpoints, including computers, mobile devices, and any systems used to access Company’s network or data, comply with industry best practices for security.
Contractor shall enforce device encryption, up-to-date antivirus protection, and endpoint detection and response (EDR) solutions on all devices used in the performance of Contractor’s obligations.
Contractor shall ensure that all endpoints are patched and updated regularly in accordance with applicable security policies and best practices.
1.2 Security Awareness Training

Contractor shall ensure that all employees, subcontractors, and personnel accessing Company’s systems or data receive annual security awareness training, including but not limited to phishing awareness, password security, and data protection.
Contractor shall maintain records of training completion and provide such records to Company upon request.
1.3 Access Controls
Contractor shall implement least privilege access controls to restrict personnel’s access to Company’s information and systems based on job function and necessity.
Contractor shall promptly revoke access to Company’s systems for any personnel who no longer require such access.
2. Personnel Security Responsibilities
Contractor shall be solely responsible for ensuring that all personnel assigned to perform services under the Agreement meet the following requirements:
2.1 Employment and Confidentiality Agreements

Contractor shall require all employees and subcontractors assigned to perform services for Company to sign employment agreements or contracts that include confidentiality, non-disclosure, and intellectual property protection provisions consistent with Company’s policies.
Contractor shall maintain executed copies of such agreements and provide confirmation of compliance to Company upon request.
2.2 Background Checks
Contractor shall conduct pre-employment background checks on all personnel assigned to perform services for Company. Background checks shall include, at a minimum:
Criminal history check in relevant jurisdictions.
Verification of identity and eligibility to work.
Employment history and reference checks.
Contractor shall not assign any personnel with a history of fraud, theft, or other relevant offenses that may pose a security risk to Company.
2.3 Policy Acknowledgment
Contractor shall ensure that all personnel assigned to work on Company projects acknowledge and comply with all applicable Company security and compliance policies, including but not limited to:
Information security policies
Acceptable use policies
Data protection and privacy policies
Confidentiality and non-disclosure requirements
Contractor shall provide Company with written confirmation that all assigned personnel have reviewed and acknowledged these policies prior to accessing any Company systems or data.
3. Compliance and Audit Rights

Contractor agrees to maintain records demonstrating compliance with the security and personnel obligations outlined in this Amendment and shall make such records available for review upon Company’s reasonable request.
Company reserves the right to conduct security audits or assessments of Contractor’s security and personnel compliance measures, subject to reasonable prior notice.
4. Term and Effect
Except as specifically modified by this Amendment, all terms and conditions of the Agreement remain in full force and effect.
This Amendment shall be binding upon and inure to the benefit of the parties and their respective successors and assigns.
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, the parties have executed this Amendment as of the Effective Date.

cookie-policy.x: Cookie Policy
Effective Date: [Date] | Last Reviewed: [Date]
Applies to: [company website] and other [Company Name] online services that link to this policy.
Application

This Cookie Policy applies to visitors and users of [company website] and any other website or online service operated by [Company Name] that links to this policy. It covers individuals located in the United States, the European Union (EU) and the European Economic Area (EEA), and residents of California. This policy aligns with applicable privacy regulations, including the GDPR and the ePrivacy Directive for EU/EEA residents and the CCPA, as amended by the CPRA, for California residents. It should be read alongside our Privacy Policy at [company website]/privacy-policy.
Policy

[Company Name] values transparency in data collection and usage. This policy outlines our use of cookies and similar technologies to enhance user experience and support [Company Name]'s operational needs. Capitalized terms not defined here have meanings as set forth in our Privacy Policy, which includes additional data collection and usage details.
What is a Cookie?

Cookies are small text files sent to your device by [Company Name] to enable specific features. They are unique to your account or browser. Session-based cookies last only while your browser is open, while persistent cookies remain until you delete them or they expire.
Does [Company Name] Use Cookies?

Yes, [Company Name] uses cookies and similar technologies, such as single-pixel gifs and web beacons. We employ both session-based and persistent cookies, along with third-party cookies like Google Analytics. These cookies are used on domains operated by [Company Name] and its affiliates.
How We Use Cookies
Cookies help [Company Name] recognize you when you return to our sites, remember preferences, and deliver a personalized experience. They also support analytics, customization, and security.
Categories of Cookies
Authentication: Enables personalized experiences based on account status.
Security: Supports security features and helps detect malicious activity.
Preferences & Features: Tracks preferred language and settings, eases form completion, and customizes content.
Marketing: Assists in tracking campaign effectiveness and user engagement.
Performance & Analytics: Enhances site performance monitoring and product improvement through user behavior insights.
Third-Party Cookies
For a list of third-party cookies [Company Name] uses and their purposes, visit our cookie tables in Appendix A below. We strive to keep this list updated, but cookie names and details may change.
Advertising Cookies
Cookies and similar technologies help us reach users interested in our services and support aggregated auditing, research, and reporting.
Managing Cookies

You can accept, decline, or change your cookie choices at any time using our Cookie Preferences centre, reachable from the Cookie Settings link in the footer of every page, or via your browser settings. Strictly necessary cookies cannot be switched off. Performance, analytics, and marketing cookies are set only after you give consent, and you can withdraw that consent at any time by reopening Cookie Settings. Note that blocking cookies may affect site functionality.

SStrictly Necessary Cookies

These cookies are necessary for the website to function and cannot be switched off in our systems. They are usually only set in response to actions made by you which amount to a request for services, such as setting your privacy preferences, logging in or filling in forms. You can set your browser to block or alert you about these cookies, but that will cause some parts of the site to not work. These cookies do not store any personally identifiable information.
Performance Cookies

These cookies (the [Company Name] uses Google Analytics) allow us to count visits and traffic sources so we can measure and improve the performance of our site. They help us to know which pages are the most and least popular and see how visitors move around the site. If you do not allow these cookies we will not know when you have visited our site and will not be able to monitor its performance.
To view an overview of the privacy of your Google Analytics cookies please go here: https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/6004245.
You may install a Google Analytics opt-out browser add-on by going here: https://tools.google.com/dlpage/gaoptout?hl=en-GB.
Marketing Cookies

We also use a marketing database management program ([MARKETING PLATFORM - [Company] to confirm]) that deploys a cookie when a user interacts with marketing communications, such as a marketing email or a marketing-based landing page on our website. This cookie collects personal information such as your name, which pages you visit on our website, how you arrived at our website, and your purchases from the [Company Name]. Collected information is used to evaluate the effectiveness of our marketing campaigns or to provide better targeting for marketing. From time to time, cookies set by third parties find their way into this “Marketing” category, but the [Company Name] does not always have control over those cookies and does not share personal data with those third parties.
Controlling and Deleting Cookies

Most cookies can be managed through your browser settings or through our Cookie Settings preference centre. Every major browser (Chrome, Safari, Firefox, and Edge) lets you view, block, and delete cookies, and most offer a private browsing mode. Deleting cookies may remove collected data, but any remaining data will no longer be tracked. Clearing your browser cookies also clears your saved consent choices, so the cookie banner will appear again on your next visit.
Contact Us

If you have questions about this Cookie Policy or about how we use cookies, contact us at [contact email], call [phone number], or write to [Company Name], [company address]. We review this policy at least annually, and whenever we add or remove cookies or tracking technologies.[contact email]

disposal-certificate.x: PROOF OF MEDIA / DEVICE DISPOSAL
Internal Audit Evidence Email Cycle - Zero-Disposal Scenario
Reusable across organizations and security frameworks (SOC 2, ISO/IEC 27001, HIPAA, PCI DSS, or other applicable requirements)
Purpose

This template provides a simple, internal email exchange that stands on its own as audit evidence when no physical media or device disposal occurred during an audit period. It is intended for direct use by the client organization's own team - no external GRC or audit party is part of the chain - and can be dropped into [GRC platform], or any evidence repository, as a self-contained artifact.
For scenarios where disposal did occur, use your organization's full disposal register and certificate-based evidence process instead of this template.
When to Use This Template
No physical media, devices, or hardware containing confidential or restricted data were disposed of, decommissioned, or destroyed during the audit period.
The organization can confirm this from an internal system of record (asset inventory, CMDB, ITSM, or equivalent).
The applicable framework allows the control/test to be marked Not Applicable when supported by evidence of zero activity (rather than requiring a certificate of destruction).
Email Cycle Overview

dr-tabletop.x: Incident Response
Overview
Use of these scenarios is appropriate in test cases where the exercise will look to evaluate the incident response plan.
Scenario: Ransomware Infection
Incident Details:

A member of the Finance Team indicated that their laptop was infected with ransomware after clicking on a malicious email attachment. There is potentially sensitive customer PII contained on the laptop, including a spreadsheet with bank and customer bank routing information. It is believed that most critical data is also located in online copies in a protected cloud share. The Incident Response Plan was fully activated in response to this incident, IT Operations and Security Staff were notified 4 hours after the incident via a text message to one of the IT Team members; this individual then escalated via email.
Immediate Impact:

The laptop’s files are unavailable pending containment and recovery. Customer PII, including bank account and routing information, may be at risk; the scenario does not establish that the data was exfiltrated. The four-hour delay in notifying IT and Security could extend the time before containment. If protected cloud copies are intact, operations may be restored from them after integrity checks. Potential consequences include disruption to Finance work, fraudulent use of exposed banking data, customer notification or regulatory obligations, and reputational harm.
Scenario: DDoS Attack on Primary Infrastructure
Scenario Background:

The organization relies on a suite of internally developed business applications to support daily operations including client management, order processing, reporting, and internal communications. These applications are hosted in a secure, cloud-based environment and are accessed by teams across departments. The architecture includes layered security measures such as web application firewalls, rate limiting, and CDN-based protections. Despite these defenses, the applications remain critical points of vulnerability, particularly to external threats such as denial-of-service attacks that can disrupt access and affect business continuity.
Incident Details:

Monitoring tools detected a significant increase in incoming traffic targeting the public-facing endpoints of several core internal business applications. The pattern matched a coordinated Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attack originating from multiple regions. Within minutes, service availability deteriorated, and application access became unreliable for internal users. The attack overwhelmed the WAF and rate-limiting protections, triggering automated alerts and failover mechanisms. The security team immediately began mitigation procedures using cloud-based DDoS protection tools and manual filtering rules to limit exposure.
Immediate Impact:

The DDoS attack rendered multiple business-critical applications inaccessible for approximately 12 hours. Internal teams were unable to complete time-sensitive tasks, including client communications, order fulfillment, and incident tracking. Productivity dropped across departments relying on these systems for operational continuity. Manual workarounds were implemented where possible, and essential services were prioritized for restoration. Although no data loss occurred, the disruption prompted increased support tickets and internal escalations. The disaster recovery team initiated post-event reviews and began planning long-term improvements to application-layer DDoS defenses and incident response automation.
Disaster Recovery and Business Continuity
Scenario: Natural Disaster_power Outage
Scenario Background:

Our [City]-based facility serves as a central hub for staff operations and resource management, including critical functions such as product delivery coordination, logistics, and customer support. The facility is equipped with on-premise infrastructure, internal servers, and physical resource handling systems that support both digital and operational workflows. While some remote work capabilities exist, the facility is the primary location for operations management, making it vital to business continuity. The disaster recovery plan accounts for scenarios involving physical disruptions, including natural disasters, power failures, and infrastructure outages that may impede facility access and staff productivity.
Incident Details:

A severe infrastructure failure, caused by a prolonged regional power outage and related utility disruptions, rendered the [City] facility completely inoperable. Essential systems, including internet access, on-premise inventory and documents, and communication lines, were affected. Staff were forced to transition to remote work within 24 hours of the outage declaration. Logistics operations and document delivery scheduling were disrupted, as access to physical inventory management systems and coordination tools was lost. This incident is projected to last five business days, during which time continuity measures outlined in the disaster recovery plan were initiated to support decentralized operations.
Immediate Impact:

The immediate impact included a halt in all on-site operations, delays in product delivery schedules, and decreased operational efficiency due to limited access to in-facility tools. Staff working remotely experienced increased dependency on cloud-based communication and coordination platforms. Customers experienced delays in shipment confirmations and support response times. Contingency actions - such as load redistribution to alternative facilities, virtual coordination of delivery schedules, and IT support for remote connectivity - were activated to minimize disruption. While full recovery and facility reoccupation were anticipated after five days, a long-term assessment of facility readiness and resilience enhancements was initiated concurrently.
Scenario: AWS Fail-Over (Or other cloud provider)

Scenario Background:Your company’s complete set of automated appointment scheduling, payment processing, same-business-day transfer, client management, and built-in marketing solutions was designed to empower beauty and wellness professionals to focus on being creators, not admins. The platform supports thousands of professionals across the country and is built for scale using a microservices architecture in AWS. Core operational data - including appointments, client records, and payment history - is housed in a centralized monolithic datastore. The system includes an active-passive failover design across two AWS regions, but real-world DR response hasn’t been fully exercised under live pressure.

Incident Details:At 2:13 AM on a weekday, your primary AWS region experiences a widespread outage that disrupts connectivity to core services. At first, it looks like a temporary blip, but after 30 minutes, key services - including appointment scheduling, payment processing, and client management - are completely unresponsive. Monitoring alerts confirm that the monolithic datastore is offline and inaccessible. As your engineering team begins executing the failover plan to the passive AWS region, they discover that the last fully replicated snapshot is three hours old due to a misconfiguration in the backup sync schedule. Now leadership must decide: restore from the available snapshot to get the platform back up quickly, or delay recovery efforts in hopes that the primary region comes back online and full data can be salvaged.

Immediate Impact:Professionals using your platform are unable to view or manage appointments, process payments, or communicate with clients, resulting in widespread cancellations and lost revenue. Same-day transfers are paused, leading to financial disruptions for many users who rely on them. Internally, pressure builds as customer service teams are overwhelmed, stakeholders demand recovery timelines, and key business partners begin escalating concerns.

A single register of every information security and availability incident, from detection to verified closure. It is the primary evidence an ISO 27001:2022 or SOC 2 auditor will sample when testing incident management.
The Security Lead owns the register. Anyone may raise an incident; only the incident owner and security lead update the record after triage.
Create a row as soon as an event is suspected - do not wait for confirmation. A false positive that is logged and closed is good evidence; an unlogged real incident is a finding.
Use INC-YYYY-NNN, sequential, never reused (for example INC-2026-001). Never delete or renumber a row; close it as 'Closed - false positive' instead.
Record date and time in a single consistent time zone (UTC recommended) using YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM. The elapsed-time columns calculate automatically.
Within the acknowledgement SLA, set Severity, Category, Data Involved and CIA Impact using the Severity & Reference tab. Assign an incident owner by name, not a team alias.
Record containment, eradication and recovery actions as they happen, with the time each was completed. Contemporaneous notes carry far more weight than notes written after closure.
For every SEV1 and SEV2, assess the notification triggers on the reference tab and record the outcome even when the answer is 'no notification required' - the assessment itself is the evidence.
Hold a blameless post-incident review for every SEV1 and SEV2 and complete the Post-Incident Review tab. Record the root cause, not the symptom.

Every root cause gets at least one corrective action with a named owner and a due date. Do not close an incident because the immediate issue went away - close it when the corrective action is verified effective.
Closure requires: root cause recorded, corrective actions complete or formally tracked, PIR held where required, reviewer named and review date set.

termination-checklist.x: Employee Termination Checklist
High-Level Process
☐ Head of People preps termination paperwork (e.g. termination agreement, reaffirmation of confidentiality and IP assignment, final expense report).
☐ Terminated employee is dismissed in Rippling - this is the trigger event; [GRC platform] syncs the termination from Rippling (typically within an hour) and opens the offboarding record.
☐ Communicate to relevant stakeholders and identify hand-off plans, including reassignment of customer, court, and agency relationships and hand-off of open cases across
☐ Remove logical and physical access and retain evidence to show SLAs were met (see checklist below).
☐ Return hardware and sanitize as needed, including [GRC platform] agent removal (see [GRC platform] Offboarding below).
☐ Wrap up financial items (e.g. credit cards, last paycheck, 401K, equity).
☐ Confirm the offboarding record is marked complete in [GRC platform].
Systems Deactivation
Logical Access to Systems - Responsible Parties: [Name] (CTO) & System Owners
☐ Identity Provider: Google Workspace (Identity Provider & Email / Drive)
☐ Version Control: GitHub (Source Code & Version Control)
☐ Cloud Infrastructure: Google Cloud Platform (GCP) & Amazon Web Services (AWS)
☐ HRIS: Rippling (HRIS & Device Management)
☐ Task Trackers: Asana & Jira
☐ Messaging & Communications: Slack
☐ Data Warehousing & Databases: Google BigQuery / GCP Cloud SQL
☐ MDM & Device Security: Rippling MDM / [GRC platform] Device Monitor
☐ Application Monitoring: Sentry
☐ MFA: Google Workspace 2-Step Verification (2SV)
☐ Compliance Platform: [GRC platform] (Console access)
☐ Access to PHI and Case Records: Revoke every role that grants access to youth, family, or case data. [Company] is HIPAA-compliant, so this is the highest-priority revocation and must be evidenced.
☐ Mobile App Distribution: Apple App Store Connect, Google Play Console
☐ Customer-Facing Systems: Support/ticketing, CRM (HubSpot), and any state or agency customer portals held.
☐ Password Manager / Shared Credentials: Revoke vault access and rotate any shared secrets the employee could view.
☐ Additional SaaS Applications: HubSpot, Notion, Zoom, Calendly, DocuSign, Anthropic, OpenAI, Dropbox, Figma, Loom, Twilio, SendGrid, A2 Hosting, [internal admin portal].
Physical Access
Responsible Parties: [Name] (Head of People) & Office Management
☐ Remove access to [office location].
☐ Data Center Access: N/A - [Company] operates 100% cloud-hosted infrastructure on GCP/AWS and maintains no physical data centers.
☐ On-Premises Servers: N/A - [Company] maintains no on-premises servers; all infrastructure is cloud-native.
Hardware
Responsible Parties: [Name] (Head of People) & IT
☐ Collect Laptop.
☐ Collect Keyboard & Mouse.
☐ Collect any other electronics (monitors, adapters, cables).
☐ Collect Office keys / keycards / badges.
☐ Stop [GRC platform] device monitoring for the returned device, then uninstall the [GRC platform] agent from the device.
☐ Wipe and sanitize the device; retain evidence that full-disk encryption was enabled at the time of return.
[GRC platform] Offboarding & Device Agent

☐ Confirm the termination synced to [GRC platform] from Rippling or the identity provider. If the record did not sync, initiate offboarding manually in [GRC platform]. HRIS data takes priority over IdP status.
☐ Review the accounts [GRC platform] surfaces: automatically deprovisioned, manually-handled, and systems flagged by group membership.
☐ Assign a deprovisioning owner to each manually-handled account. [GRC platform] defaults to the vendor's security owner - confirm the default is correct before accepting it.
☐ Owners complete their tasks under Access > Deprovisioning tasks and confirm each account is deprovisioned.
☐ The [GRC platform] agent is required on every [Company]-managed endpoint. On termination, stop monitoring for the returned device in [GRC platform].
☐ Uninstall the [GRC platform] agent from the device before it is wiped, decommissioned, or reissued. Removing a device in [GRC platform] only stops monitoring - it does not uninstall the agent.
☐ Mark the record fully offboarded in [GRC platform] once all required tasks are complete.
Evidence & SLAs
• Record the exact date and time of each access revocation.
• Target SLA: Privileged and PHI-bearing access revoked within 24 hours of termination effective time; all remaining system access revoked within 3 business days (72 hours).
• Retain screenshots or system exports as evidence that the SLA was met - this is the required artifact for SOC 2 and HIPAA audits.
• Attach the completed checklist and revocation evidence to the employee's offboarding record in [GRC platform] and Rippling.
